newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault boss to meet staff representatives.
newsitem.headline: Renault boss to meet staff representatives.

text.p: Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer will meet this week with representatives of a Belgian assembly plant slated for closure, a company spokeswoman said on Monday.
She said Renault had no comment on newspaper reports it was preparing to announce a plan to cut some 3,000 jobs in France.
An official with the CGT union said Schweitzer was also expected to make a rare appearance at a staff works meeting in France on Thursday.

"Schweitzer has let it be known that he'll explain the situation the company finds itself in on Thursday at an extraordinary staff works council meeting," the official with France's Communist-led CGT, Renault's biggest union, told Reuters.
The spokeswoman said Schweitzer had agreed to meet with staff representatives of the Vilvoorde plant near Brussels this week but the time and place were not fixed.
She also said the agenda for the staff works meeting in France on Thursday was not set.

French newspapers report that Renault plans to accelerate its job cutting programme and will announce some 3,000 job cuts for 1997, after 1,641 in 1996, 1,735 in 1995, 2,109 in 1994 and 2,249 in 1993. The biggest single-year cut took place in 1992, when 3,700 jobs were eliminated.
The Force Ouvriere union said in a statement last week that it feared 3,000 jobs could be cut in France this year, but union officials contacted by Reuters on Monday had not seen such a plan.
Renault has four assembly plants in France, Douai, Maubeuge, Flins, and Sandouville, two in Spain, in Valladolid and Palencia, the Setubal plant in Portugal and Novo Mesto in Slovenia.
Representatives of several unions will meet today to discuss possible action, the CGT official said. They will include representatives of Spanish workers but not Belgian ones.

Newspapers said the charges for the job-cutting plans, on top of an operating loss at the group estimated at two billion francs or more, would result in a full year loss of more than five billion francs for the group in 1996.
The afternoon daily Le Monde said the job cuts would include many early retirements.
